desc:
Place a binary tree on a complete binary tree frame: the root has slot 1, and a node in slot p has its left child in slot 2p and its right child in slot 2p + 1. The width of a level is (slot of its rightmost node) - (slot of its leftmost node) + 1 (missing nodes between the ends count), and the width of the tree is the largest width of any level. The empty tree has width 0.

Before measuring, you may pick any set of nodes and, for each picked node, swap its left and right child (a missing child is swapped too, so a lone left child can become a lone right child). A swap moves the complete subtrees. Return the largest tree width that can be reached.

How trees are given. There is no tree type here. A binary tree is passed as an integer array in level-order (top to bottom, left to right), the same way LeetCode serialises trees. A missing child is written as -1, and every real node value is non-negative. The children of a missing node are not listed, and trailing -1 entries are dropped, so a non-empty array never ends with -1. The empty tree is [].

For example, [1, 2, 3, -1, 4] describes the tree on the left: the root is 1 with children 2 and 3, node 2 has no left child and has 4 as its right child, and node 3 is a leaf.

    1
   / \
  2   3
   \
    4

For tree = [1, 2, 3, 4, -1, 5, -1, 6, -1, 7] (two chains hanging below the root) the last level holds the nodes 6 and 7 in slots 8 and 12, so the width is 5. Swapping the children of node 3 and of node 5 moves 7 to slot 15, giving width 8, and no arrangement does better, so the answer is 8. For tree = [1, 2, -1, 3], a single path, every level has one node and the answer is 1.
constraints: The array follows the encoding above exactly (valid level-order, no trailing -1)
The tree has at most 30 levels, so every width fits in a 32-bit integer
hints: A wide level needs two far apart nodes on one level. Where do the paths from the root to two such nodes separate?

Let the two nodes separate at a node a that has children in both directions. Below a the two paths share no node, so you can choose the swaps on them independently: swapping at a puts one node to the left side, and swaps further down can push that node to the far left of its half and the other to the far right of its half.

If both nodes are k levels below a, the width is exactly 2k (from the leftmost to the rightmost slot below a on that level), independent of everything above a. The deepest common level below a is limited by the shorter of its two child subtrees.
editorial: Take any level and two of its nodes u and v, and let a be their lowest common ancestor, k levels above them. The slots of u and v agree on all bits that come from the path root → a; after that, u goes into one child subtree of a and v into the other, and then each follows a path made of choices that belong to nodes only on its own side. Using the swap at a we put u on the left, and swaps along the path of u make every step go left (any node on the path has at most one child on that path, and a swap decides whether it is the left or the right one), so u gets the smallest possible slot A · 2k. In the same way v gets the largest slot A · 2k + 2k - 1. The width of the level is therefore exactly 2k, whatever the shape above a.

So we want a node a with two children and the largest k such that both child subtrees reach k - 1 edges below the children. With h(x) the height of the subtree of x in edges, the best value for a is k = 1 + min(h(left), h(right)). The answer is 21 + M with M the maximum of min(h(left), h(right)) over all nodes that have two children. If no node has two children the tree is a single path and every level has one node, so the answer is 1 (and 0 for the empty tree). Heights come from one backwards pass over the level-order array, so the time is O(n).
